public_rationale: TIME reported on January 18, 2023 that OpenAI valued its November 2021–March 2022 Sama partnership contracts at about $150,000 [e1]. This is a reported contract value, not a verified payment total [e1]. It neither establishes nor rules out vast industry spending on human corrective work between January 1, 2020 and February 3, 2023 [e1].
limitations: The evidence covers one partnership and provides neither aggregate realized expenditure nor budget context for judging the industry's spending scale [e1].
The contract value does not establish the comparison with spending on symbolic systems in the 1980s [e1].

public_payload.normalized_proposition: In the 2020s, AI companies spend vast sums hiring humans to patch brittle neural systems, as companies did for symbolic systems in the 1980s.

statement.excerpt: 2020s: AI companies spend vast amounts of $ hiring humans to to patch brittle neural systems.
statement.document_title: Happy Groundhog Day, The AI Edition

our_interpretation: The explicit 2020s period means the decade to the publication date, not spending after the post.
The plain reading is substantial industry expenditure on human feedback and corrective training work, rather than merely the existence of paid contractors.
The accompanying industry commentary supplies an estimate-based framing, not a stated financial-reporting standard.
The dollar symbol is read as US dollars in this US-company context.
The comparison with symbolic AI is an analogy. The exact claim does not commit to equal spending across the two eras.
The quoted prediction of future hundreds of millions or billions is not evidence of spending already incurred.
criteria.support_condition: Credible expenditure records or well-founded estimates show substantial spending across AI companies on human corrective work during the stated period, with enough budget context to justify the ordinary description vast.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comprehensive, comparable expenditure evidence shows that such spending was minor in scale, or that the expenditure attributed to human corrective work was actually for other purposes.
